rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Manʿ, ṣadd, and ḥaylūla are synonyms; the opposite of prevention is release. Manīʿ means inaccessible or protected, and manīʿa describes a woman who will not yield to lewdness.
rows.anchor: المنع والصد والحيلولة نظائر وضد المنع الإطلاق يقال منعته فامتنع ورجل منيع أي لا يخلص إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saʿy is synonymous with running and racing, opposite to stopping; seeking livelihood means earning for one's family, while seeking authority may mean administering charity. A couplet uses saʿā for collecting annual alms.
rows.anchor: والسعي والركض والعدو نظائر وضد السعي الوقف وفلان يسعى على عياله أي يكسب لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom sāʿā al-ama means a man committed fornication with a slave woman; musāʿāt is used only of slave women.
rows.anchor: وساعى الرجل الأمة إذا فجر بها ولا تكون المساعاة إلا في الإماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kharāb, demolition, and dismantling are synonyms. Kharba is a broad earlobe piercing or any round hole.
rows.anchor: والخراب والهدم والنقض نظائر والخربة سعة خرق الأذن وكل ثقب مستدير

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī says khārib means a thief, specifically a camel thief, and khirāba is camel theft.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي: يختص بسارق الإبل والخرابة سرقة الإبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min is interrogative and occupies a nominative position; aẓlam is the predicate of the initial subject.
rows.anchor: موضع من رفع وهو استفهام وأظلم رفع لأنه خبر الابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An is an accusative appositional replacement for masājid, specifically a بدل اشتمال construction.
rows.anchor: موضع أن نصب على البدل من مساجد وهو بدل الاشتمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, an is an accusative object of purpose: they prevented worship because they disliked God's name being mentioned there.
rows.anchor: أن نصبا على أنه مفعول له فيكون تقديره كراهة أن يذكر فيها اسمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis supplies a deleted min, giving the sense of preventing people from mentioning God's name there.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون على حذف من وتقديره من أن يذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An yadkhulūhā is the nominative subject of kāna; alternatively, kāna is redundant and the clause is an initial subject.
rows.anchor: وأن يدخلوها في موضع رفع بأنه اسم كان وقيل إن كان ها هنا مزيدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Illā here cancels the preceding negation, and khāʾifīn is an accusative circumstantial qualifier.
rows.anchor: وإلا حرف الاستثناء وهو هنا لنقض النفي وخائفين منصوب على الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khizy is nominative either as a subject or because of the preceding lam; the phrases in this world and in the next function as circumstantial qualifiers of the implicit subject in lahum.
rows.anchor: وقوله خزي مرفوع من وجهين أحدهما: الابتداء والآخر:

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī rejects the Quraysh identification because they did not physically demolish the Sacred Mosque; mosque ruin means preventing prayer, and reports describe their destruction of prayer sites in Mecca.
rows.anchor: الطبري بأن قال إن مشركي قريش لم يسعوا في تخريب المسجد الحرام

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī also says the Quraysh reading fits the preceding rebuke of the People of the Book less well than the reading about Christians and Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: وهو أيضا لا يتعلق بما قبله من ذم أهل الكتاب كما يتعلق به إذا عنى به النصارى وبيت المقدس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author answers the contextual objection: verse 2:113 had already mentioned people who lack knowledge, and the condemnation can alternate among Jews, Christians, and idolaters.
rows.anchor: وهذا أقرب لأن الكلام خرج مخرج الذم فمرة توجه الذم إلى اليهود ومرة إلى النصارى

words: مَّنَعَ مَسَٰجِدَ ٱللَّهِ أَن يُذْكَرَ فِيهَا ٱسْمُهُۥ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one is more unjust than one who stops God's name being mentioned in His mosques and prevents congregational prayer and worship there.
rows.anchor: لا أحد أظلم ممن منع أن يذكر في مساجد الله اسمه سبحانه وعمل في المنع من إقامة الجماعة والعبادة فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the plural means Jerusalem or the Kaaba, it can denote the many prostration places within a great mosque, the whole mosque, or all mosques built by Muslims.
rows.anchor: فإنما جاز جمعه على أحد وجهين إما أن تكون مواضع السجود فإن المسجد العظيم يقال لكل موضع منه مسجد

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī transmits from his forefathers, from ʿAlī, that the phrase means the whole earth, based on the Prophet's teaching that the earth is a mosque and its soil a purifier.
rows.anchor: وروي عن زيد بن علي عن آبائه عن علي ع أنه أراد جميع الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ruining a mosque can mean expelling believers during migration, barring them from it, or preventing prayer and obedience there; both first senses may apply.
rows.anchor: أي عمل في تخريبها والتخريب إخراجهم أهل الإيمان منها عند الهجرة وقيل هو صدهم عنها ويجوز حمله على الأمرين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Christians may enter Jerusalem only after severe beating and punishment, as remains the case today.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس معناه أنه لا يدخل نصراني بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: If the verse concerns the Sacred Mosque, the Prophet ordered an announcement barring polytheist pilgrimage after that year and naked circumambulation; they stopped entering afterward.
rows.anchor: أمر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم مناديا فنادى:

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī says polytheists may not enter the Sacred Mosque or other mosques, and those who enter are expelled except litigants visiting a judge briefly under fear of removal.
rows.anchor: قال الجبائي بين الله سبحانه أنه ليس لهؤلاء المشركين دخول المسجد الحرام

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar says the verse proves unbelievers may be barred from every mosque and polytheists from the Sacred Mosque even for litigation; 9:17 and 9:28 support the latter rule.
rows.anchor: قال الشيخ أبو جعفر قدس الله روحه

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj interprets this as God's promise of Muslim ascendancy, such that opponents cannot enter their mosques except fearfully, paralleling 9:33.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج أعلم الله سبحانه في هذه الآية

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says worldly humiliation is payment of the poll tax in a state of subjection.
rows.anchor: أحدها: أن يراد بالخزي أنهم يعطون الجزية عن يد وهم صاغرون عن قتادة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says humiliation entails killing and captivity when they are at war, or poll tax when they are protected subjects.
rows.anchor: وثانيها: أن المراد به القتل وسبي الذراري والنساء إن كانوا حربا وإعطاء الجزية إن كانوا ذمة عن الزجاج

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says the Mahdi will kill them after rising and conquering Constantinople.
rows.anchor: وثالثها: إن المراد بخزيهم في الدنيا أنه إذا قام المهدي وفتح قسطنطينية فحينئذ يقتلهم عن السدي

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says their humiliation is exclusion from mosques.
rows.anchor: ورابعها: أن المراد بخزيهم طردهم عن دخول المساجد عن أبي علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Judgment Day they will be punished in Hell with the greatest punishment, because they are the most unjust of wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: يعني يوم القيامة يعذبهم الله في نار جهنم بالعذاب الأعظم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Muslims faced Jerusalem for seventeen months after the Prophet arrived in Medina.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس كانت الصلاة إلى بيت المقدس بعد مقدم النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم المدينة سبعة عشر شهرا

rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib reports praying with the Prophet toward Jerusalem for sixteen or seventeen months before they were turned toward the Kaaba; Muslim includes the report in his Ṣaḥīḥ.
rows.anchor: عن البراء بن عازب قال:

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas ibn Mālik gives the Jerusalem prayer period as nine or ten months.
rows.anchor: وعن أنس بن مالك: إنما كان ذلك تسعة أشهر أو عشرة أشهر

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: Muʿādh ibn Jabal gives the period as thirteen months.
rows.anchor: وعن معاذ بن جبل ثلاثة عشر شهرا

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: A report from al-Ṣādiq says the Prophet faced Jerusalem for thirteen years in Mecca and seven months in Medina; Jews taunted him, so he grieved and awaited revelation. Gabriel turned him toward the Kaaba during noon prayer at Banū Sālim's mosque after two rakʿas; he completed two facing the Kaaba, prompting Jewish and foolish criticism.
rows.anchor: ورواه علي بن إبراهيم بإسناده عن الصادق ع قال:

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj explains that Jerusalem was initially appointed because Arabs were accustomed to pilgrimage to the Kaaba; God tested who would follow the Messenger despite a different direction.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: إنما أمر بالصلاة إلى بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance means directing someone to the religion; it is called a straight path because it leads to Paradise, the destination.
rows.anchor: أي يدله ويرشده إلى الدين وإنما سماه الصراط لأنه طريق الجنة المؤدي إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ruʾya first means visual perception, like seeing, and is also used for knowledge.
rows.anchor: الرؤية هي إدراك الشيء بالبصر ونظيره الإبصار ثم تستعمل بمعنى العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqallub, change, and disposition are synonyms describing movement in different directions.
rows.anchor: والتقلب والتحول والتصرف نظائر وهو التحرك في الجهات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wallaytuka al-qibla means I made you face the qibla; the verb here is distinct from walaytu al-dār, which only means that a house adjoins another.
rows.anchor: ويقال وليتك القبلة أي صيرتك تستقبلها بوجهك وليس هذا المعنى في فعلت منه لأنك تقول وليت الدار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb is also used for turning one's back, as in 54:45 and 3:111, from expressions meaning that one side of a house lies next to another or that someone turns toward a side.
rows.anchor: وقد جاءت هذه الكلمة مستعملة على خلاف المقابلة والمواجهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Riḍā and love are near in meaning but contrasted with different opposites: love with hatred, satisfaction with displeasure; divine satisfaction signifies willing honor and reward.
rows.anchor: والرضا والمحبة نظيران وإنما يظهر الفرق بضديهما فالمحبة ضدها البغض والرضا ضده السخط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shatr means toward or in the direction of; a cited couplet uses it for toward a border or target.
rows.anchor: وشطر المسجد الحرام أي نحوه وتلقاءه

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says shāṭarūnā means that people's houses adjoin ours; yanāḥūnanā similarly means we are oriented toward one another.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: يقال هؤلاء القوم مشاطرونا أي دورهم تتصل بدورنا

rows.speaker: صاحب العين
rows.claim: Ṣāḥib al-ʿAyn says shatr can mean half or direction and aim; an idiom uses it for half a milking, and shatartu means divided something.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب العين: شطر كل شيء نصفه وشطره نحوه وقصده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥarām means forbidden, just as kitāb means written and ḥisāb means reckoned.
rows.anchor: والحرام المحرم كما أن الكتاب بمعنى المكتوب والحساب بمعنى المحسوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥaqq is putting a thing in its proper place where there is no aspect of ugliness.
rows.anchor: والحق وضع الشيء في موضعه إذا لم يكن فيه وجه من وجه القبح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghafla is inattention to particular things; broad inattention is more extensive, and calling a sleeper heedless is figurative.
rows.anchor: والغفلة هي السهو عن بعض الأشياء خاصة وإذا كان السهو عاما فهو فوق الغفلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥaythumā kuntum is conditional, with the sense wherever you may be; its response is fa-wallū and what follows. Ḥaythu and idhā need mā to detach them from their following clause and enable conditional jussive syntax.
rows.anchor: حيث ما كنتم موضع كنتم جزم بالشرط وتقديره وحيثما تكونوا والفاء وما بعده في موضع الجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shatrahu is accusative as an adverb of direction.
rows.anchor: وشطر منصوب على الظرف

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes report that the Kaaba was the Prophet's preferred direction. He asked Gabriel to seek a change from the Jewish qibla; Gabriel told him to pray to God, and the Prophet watched the sky awaiting revelation.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون كانت الكعبة أحب القبلتين إلى رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sees Muhammad looking toward the sky while he awaits revelation about the qibla.
rows.anchor: يا محمد { في السماء } لانتظار الوحي في أمر القبلة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One explanation says the Prophet had been promised a change of qibla and looked toward the expected source of the awaited revelation, as people watch for what they expect.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أنه كان وعد بتحويل القبلة عن بيت المقدس فكان يفعل ذلك انتظارا وتوقعا للموعود

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says he disliked Jerusalem and favored the Kaaba but could not ask God without permission: prophets must not request what they have not been authorized to ask, lest its refusal become a trial for their people.
rows.anchor: والثاني: أنه كان يكره قبلة بيت المقدس ويهوى قبلة الكعبة وكان لا يسأل الله تعالى ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet wanted the Kaaba because it was the qibla of his forefather Abraham and his ancestors.
rows.anchor: قبلة أبيه إبراهيم ع وقبلة آبائه عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says Jews taunted that Muhammad differed from their religion yet followed their qibla.
rows.anchor: يخالفنا محمد في ديننا ويتبع قبلتنا عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says Jews claimed Muhammad and his companions did not know their qibla until the Jews guided them.
rows.anchor: أين قبلتهم حتى هديناهم عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that Arabs deeply revered the Kaaba, so facing it would draw their hearts and make them more eager to pray toward it; the Prophet was keen to call them to Islam.
rows.anchor: كانت العرب يحبون الكعبة ويعظمونها غاية التعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author allows that all these reasons together may explain the Prophet's preference because they do not conflict.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون إنما أحب ذلك لجميع هذه الوجوه إذ لا تنافي بينها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promises to turn Muhammad toward a qibla he wants and naturally loves; this does not mean he resented the first qibla.
rows.anchor: أي فلنصرفنك إلى قبلة تريدها وتحبها وإنما أراد به محبة الطباع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turn yourself toward the Sacred Mosque: wajh can mean the person himself, and the face is named because it visibly expresses orientation.
rows.anchor: أي حول نفسك نحو المسجد الحرام لأن وجه الشيء نفسه

rows.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī takes shatr to mean half, so the command targets half of the mosque directly opposite the Kaaba; the author rejects this as contrary to the exegetes' view.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي الجبائي: أراد بالشطر النصف فأمره الله تعالى بالتوجه إلى نصف المسجد الحرام

words: وَحَيْثُ مَا كُنتُمْ فَوَلُّوا۟ وُجُوهَكُمْ شَطْرَهُۥ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wherever people are on earth—land or sea, plain or mountain—they should face the Kaaba. The first command addresses the Prophet and Medina; the second extends the qibla to every worshipper across the world.
rows.anchor: أي أينما كنتم من الأرض في بر أو بحر وسهلا سهل أو جبل فولوا وجوهكم نحوه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī quotes Ibn ʿAbbās: the House is qibla for the doorway, the House for mosque-goers, the mosque for the Sacred Precinct, and the Precinct for the whole earth. This matches the Imāmī view that the Precinct is qibla for those far away.
rows.anchor: وذكر أبو إسحاق الثعلبي في كتابه عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those given scripture refers either to Jewish scholars or to Jewish and Christian scholars together.
rows.anchor: أراد به علماء اليهود وقيل علماء اليهود والنصارى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They know that changing the qibla to the Kaaba is commanded truth from their Lord because their prophets' glad tidings described a prophet whose traits included praying toward both qiblas.
rows.anchor: أي يعلمون أن تحويل القبلة إلى الكعبة حق مأمور به من ربهم

rows.speaker: اليهود
rows.claim: The Jews objected that Muhammad had not been ordered to change direction and was inventing it himself, turning now one way and now another; the verse answers that they know this claim is false.
rows.anchor: وروي أنهم قالوا عند التحويل ما أمرت بهذا يا محمد وإنما هو شيء تبتدعه من تلقاء نفسك مرة إلى هنا ومرة إلى هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is aware of their concealment of Muhammad's description and their deliberate opposition. The addressed group must be small enough to collude and display beliefs contrary to what they know; such unified collusion is not plausible for a vast group.
rows.anchor: ليس الله بغافل عما يعمل هؤلاء من كتمان صفة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse abrogates the obligation to face Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية ناسخة لفرض التوجه إلى بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the first abrogation mentioned in the Quran was the qibla matter.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أول ما نسخ من القرآن

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says this verse abrogated what came before it.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة نسخت هذه الآية ما قبلها

rows.speaker: جعفر بن مبشر
rows.claim: Jaʿfar ibn Mubashshir says the Quran abrogated a Sunna; the author regards this as strongest because no Quranic text establishes the Jerusalem direction as obligatory.
rows.anchor: وقال جعفر بن مبشر هذا مما نسخ من السنة بالقرآن وهذا هو الأقوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the qibla verse abrogated 2:115, but the author says that verse remains operative for voluntary prayers while traveling, as reported from Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAbd Allāh.
rows.anchor: ومن قال إنها نسخت قوله:

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: One view says the Prophet prayed toward the Kaaba in Mecca, was commanded to face Jerusalem after migrating to Medina, then was turned back to the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: واختلف الناس في صلاة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إلى بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Another view says that in Mecca the Prophet faced Jerusalem while placing the Kaaba between himself and it, praying only where that alignment was possible.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم كان يصلي بمكة إلى بيت المقدس إلا أنه كان يجعل الكعبة بينه وبينها

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: A third view says the Prophet faced Jerusalem in Mecca and after arriving in Medina without needing to place the Kaaba between himself and it, until he was commanded to face the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم بل كان يصلي بمكة وبعد قدومه المدينة إلى بيت المقدس ولم يكن عليه أن يجعل

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: In some transmissions, al-Kisāʾī applies imāla to the nūn in innā and the lām in lillāh; other readers pronounce them with tafkhīm.
rows.anchor: أمال الكسائي في بعض الروايات النون من إنا واللام من لله والباقون بالتفخيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imāla is allowed in innā with God's name because of the kasra and frequent use, which make the sequence almost one word.
rows.anchor: وإنما جازت الإمالة في هذه الألف مع اسم الله للكسرة مع كثرة الاستعمال حتى صارت بمنزلة الكلمة الواحدة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says innā cannot be imāla before a name other than Allah, since particles and similar forms normally resist imāla and inflection like parts of a word.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: لا يجوز إمالة إنا مع غير الاسم الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muṣība is a hardship that strikes the soul through the harm it causes; its name derives from striking or befalling someone with a calamity.
rows.anchor: المصيبة المشقة الداخلة على النفس لما يلحقها من المضرة وهو من الإصابة كأنها تصيبها بالنكبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Returning is a thing's return to a prior state, as in a house becoming someone's property again; it is synonymous with returning and becoming.
rows.anchor: والرجوع مصير الشيء إلى ما كان يقال رجعت الدار إلى فلان إذا ملكها مرة ثانية وهو نظير العود والمصير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance means attaining the path of truth.
rows.anchor: والاهتداء الإصابة لطريق الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse describes patient people who, when struck by a personal or financial calamity, prepare themselves to bear it in hope of reward.
rows.anchor: أي نالتهم نكبة في النفس أو المال فوطنوا أنفسهم على ذلك احتسابا للأجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying we belong to God is an acknowledgment of servitude: we are His servants and property.
rows.anchor: هذا إقرار بالعبودية أي نحن عبيد الله وملكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying we return to God is an acknowledgment of resurrection and the final return to His judgment.
rows.anchor: هذا إقرار بالبعث والنشور أي نحن إلى حكمه نصير

rows.speaker: أمير المؤمنين
rows.claim: The Commander of the Faithful says the first phrase acknowledges God's ownership of us and the second acknowledges our perishing.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال أمير المؤمنين عليه السلام: إن قولنا إنا لله إقرار على أنفسنا بالملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The formula consoles because God will repair a justly incurred calamity and secure justice against its perpetrator if it was unjust; it expresses submission to His plan and trust in His judgment.
rows.anchor: وإنما كانت هذه اللفظة تعزية عن المصيبة لما فيها من الدلالة على أن الله تعالى يجبرها

words: قَالُوا۟ إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّآ إِلَيْهِ رَٰجِعُونَ
rows.speaker: الحديث
rows.claim: A hadith says that whoever says istirjāʿ when struck by calamity will have God repair the affliction, improve the outcome, and grant a pleasing righteous replacement.
rows.anchor: من استرجع عند المصيبة جبر الله مصيبته

words: قَالُوا۟ إِنَّا لِلَّهِ وَإِنَّآ إِلَيْهِ رَٰجِعُونَ
rows.speaker: أمير المؤمنين
rows.claim: The Commander of the Faithful says that even if much time has passed, saying istirjāʿ after a calamity earns the reward given on the day it occurred.
rows.anchor: من أصيب بمصيبة فأحدث استرجاعا وإن تقادم عهدها كتب الله له

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Al-Ṣādiq transmits from his forefathers, from the Prophet, that four traits qualify a person for Paradise: professing God's oneness, thanking Him for a blessing, seeking forgiveness after sin, and saying the istirjāʿ formula after calamity.
rows.anchor: وروى الصادق عليه السلام عن آبائه عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those points to the patient people described in the preceding verse.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى الذين وصفهم من الصابرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's ṣalawāt are beautiful praise and commendation, a form of purification and prayer; the term conveys permanence because praise is always deserved and prayer recurs.
rows.anchor: أي ثناء جميل من ربهم وتزكية وهو بمعنى الدعاء لأن الثناء يستحق دائما ففيه معنى اللزوم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the prayers as blessings from their Lord.
rows.anchor: وقيل بركات من ربهم عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation takes the prayers to mean forgiveness from their Lord.
rows.anchor: وقيل مغفرة من ربهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mercy is favor in this world and the next; it is favor shown to the needy, and everyone needs God's favor in both lives.
rows.anchor: أي نعمة عاجلا وآجلا فالرحمة النعمة على المحتاج وكل أحد يحتاج إلى نعمة الله في دنياه وعقباه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The patient are rightly guided by finding the true path through istirjāʿ; another view says they are guided to Paradise and reward.
rows.anchor: أي المصيبون طريق الحق في الاسترجاع وقيل وإلى الجنة والثواب

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: When ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb recited this verse, he called it an excellent pair of weights and an excellent extra load.
rows.anchor: وكان عمر بن الخطاب إذا قرأ هذه الآية قال نعم العدلان ونعمت العلاوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ajāba and istajāba both mean to answer; a couplet uses them in the same sense. Al-Mubarrad distinguishes them, saying istijāba implies acquiescence while ijāba does not.
rows.anchor: أجاب واستجاب بمعنى قال الشاعر:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root j-w-b means cutting through: one traverses a land or pierces darkness; answering cuts through a question that is suspended between yes and no.
rows.anchor: وأصله من الجوب وهو القطع يقال جاب البلاد يجوبها جوبا إذا قطعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author treats jāba, obedience, and capacity as verbal nouns; answering a question is called a response, and clouds clearing is injiāb.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أن الجابة والطاعة والطاقة ونحوها أسماء بمعنى المصادر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rushd is the opposite of error; the word has two verb forms, and rashīd describes someone soundly guided. The root means attaining good and irshād is guidance toward it.
rows.anchor: والرشد نقيض الغي رشد يرشد رشدا ورشد يرشد رشدا ورجل رشيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idhā is a temporal adverb for the implied command Tell them, as indicated by fa-innī qarīb. It cannot be governed by qarīb or ujību because an inna predicate cannot govern outside its clause; ujību is a second predicate of inna.
rows.anchor: إذا ظرف زمان للفعل الذي يدل عليه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says a questioner asked the Prophet whether their Lord was near, so they could whisper to Him, or distant, so they should call aloud; the verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: روي عن الحسن أن سائلا سأل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أقريب ربنا فنناجيه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the verse answered people who asked the Prophet how they should supplicate.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة نزلت جوابا لقوم سألوا النبي كيف ندعوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mention of supplication follows the discussion of fasting and its relation to prayer and God's response.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر سبحانه الصوم عقبه بذكر الدعاء ومكانه منه وإجابته إياه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question most likely concerns God's attribute, not an action, since the answer says He is near; an implied say introduces the reply.
rows.anchor: الأقرب أن يكون السؤال عن صفته سبحانه لا عن فعله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has no place: if He were located somewhere, He could not be near to everyone who addresses Him.
rows.anchor: فدل بهذا على أنه سبحانه لا مكان له إذ لو كان له مكان لم يكن قريبا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation takes near to mean that God answers a supplicant quickly, since nearness and speed are related.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه إني سريع الإجابة إلى دعاء الداعي لأن السريع والقريب متقاربان

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation says God hears an invoker as a nearby person hears them; nearness of distance itself is impossible for God because it belongs to created beings situated in a place.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه إني أسمع دعاء الداعي كما يسمعه القريب المسافة منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise of answering is clear in meaning.
rows.anchor: أجيب دعوة الداعي إذا دعان

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda explains the imperative as answering God in response to what He has called them to do.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: معناه فليجيبوني فيما دعوتهم إليه

rows.speaker: المبرد والسراج
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad and al-Sarrāj explain it as seeking the truth by conforming to what God commands and forbids.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد والسراج: معناه فليذهبوا للحق بطلب موافقة ما أمرتهم به

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid explains it as responding to God through obedience.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: معناه فليستجيبوا لي بالطاعة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the command to mean let them supplicate to Me.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه فليدعوني

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet calls the person who cannot supplicate the most incapable and the person who withholds greeting the most miserly.
rows.anchor: أعجز الناس من عجز عن الدعاء وأبخل الناس من بخل بالسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Belief here means affirming everything God revealed.
rows.anchor: أي وليصدقوا بجميع ما أنزلته

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abū ʿAbd Allāh explains belief as recognizing that God can grant what they request.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي عبد الله أنه قال: وليؤمنوا بي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may find the truth and be guided to it.
rows.anchor: أي لعلهم يصيبون الحق ويهتدون إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God answers supplication in a manner consistent with wisdom: the request must benefit the person's religion and harm neither the supplicant nor another; God grants it when beneficial and delays it when delay is better.
rows.anchor: ليس أحد يدعو الله على ما توجبه الحكمة إلا أجابه الله فإن الداعي إذا دعاه يجب أن يسأل ما فيه صلاح له في دينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supplication remains meaningful even when wisdom determines the outcome: it is worship expressing humility and submission, and a requested event may become beneficial only after the supplication.
rows.anchor: أن الدعاء عبادة في نفسها يعبد الله سبحانه بها لما في ذلك من إظهار الخضوع والانقياد

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reports the Prophet saying that a Muslim's prayer without sin or severing kinship receives one of three outcomes: prompt fulfillment, a reward saved for the afterlife, or equivalent harm averted. The Companions ask if they should pray more, and he answers that God is more generous.
rows.anchor: ما من مسلم دعا الله سبحانه بدعوة ليس فيها قطيعة رحم ولا إثم

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas ibn Mālik's version gives the response as God being more generous and better, repeated three times.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية أنس بن مالك:

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh reports the Prophet saying God may defer a beloved servant's request because He loves hearing the servant's voice, but quickly grant a sincere request from a servant He dislikes because He hates hearing that voice.
rows.anchor: وروي عن جابر بن عبد الله قال قال رسول الله:

rows.speaker: أمير المؤمنين
rows.claim: The Commander of the Faithful says an answer may be delayed to increase the supplicant's reward and make the eventual gift more abundant.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أمير المؤمنين ع أنه قال: ربما أخرت عن العبد

rows.speaker: إبراهيم بن أدهم
rows.claim: Asked why prayers go unanswered, Ibrāhīm ibn Adham says people know God but disobey, know the Prophet but neglect his Sunna, know the Quran but do not act on it, fail to thank blessings or seek Paradise and flee Hell, agree with Satan, neglect preparation for death, fail to learn from the dead, and occupy themselves with others' faults.
rows.anchor: وقيل لإبراهيم بن أدهم: ما بالنا ندعو الله سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Intihāʾ is abstaining; nahy is forbidding an act with a negative command and disapproval, while amr urges an act with a positive command and the commander's intent.
rows.anchor: الانتهاء الامتناع والنهي الزجر عن الفعل بصيغة لا تفعل مع كراهة الناهي لذلك الفعل والأمر الدعاء إلى الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-nahy can also mean a pond that holds back water, and the plural nuhya means intellect; tanhiya is a hollow where rainwater ends or pools, and inhāʾ brings something to its limit.
rows.anchor: والنهي الغدير لمنعه الماء أن يفيض والنهي بمنزلة المنع ونهاية الشيء غايته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maghfira is covering a sin so that, in legal judgment, it is treated as if it never occurred.
rows.anchor: والمغفرة تغطية الذنب بما يصير به بمنزلة غير الواقع في الحكم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid and others explain desisting as repenting from unbelief.
rows.anchor: أي امتنعوا من كفرهم بالتوبة منه عن مجاهد وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional clause is abbreviated because the preceding context makes its omitted content clear.
rows.anchor: فاختصر الكلام لدلالة ما تقدم من الشرط عليه

words: فَإِنِ ٱنتَهَوْا۟ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse establishes that an intentional killer's repentance is accepted: God has declared that He accepts a polytheist's repentance, and association is graver than killing.
rows.anchor: وفيه الدلالة على أنه يقبل توبة القاتل عمدا لأنه بين عز اسمه أنه يقبل توبة المشرك
